title: Scale factors for area and volume

files.lesson.md: --- order: 26 unit: enlarge9 node: AC9M9SP02 n2 uses: [AC9M9SP02 n1] assumes: [AC9M9SP02 n1] connection: scale-up-monster title: Scale factors for area and volume summary: "When lengths are multiplied by k, areas are multiplied by k² and volumes by k³. That is why a giant can't just be a bigger copy of a normal animal." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A film makes a lizard ten times bigger. Could its legs hold it up?" --- A film monster is a lizard scaled up 10 times in every direction: ten times longer, ten times wider and ten times taller. Its weight depends on its volume, and a leg's strength depends on its cross-section, an area. Have a guess which grows faster, and we'll come back to it at the end. (This is a model, not a real animal.) ## Predict: cubes in a bigger cube ```step stage: predict insight: "Counting the small cubes in a cube of side 2 shows whether students expect volume to double or to grow by the cube of the factor." check: type: predict q: "A cube with side 1 is enlarged by a scale factor of 2. How many of the small cubes does the big cube hold?" options: - "8" - "2" - "4" - "6" actual: "8. It's two layers of four cubes: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Doubling the sides makes the volume 2³ = 8 times as big." ``` ## Run: count ```step stage: run insight: "Lengths grow by k, the area of a face by k × k, and the volume by k × k × k." check: { type: number, q: "A cube has side 1. It is enlarged by a scale factor of 3. How many small cubes does it hold?", answer: 27, explain: "3 × 3 × 3 = 27." } ``` ## Investigate: k, k² and k³ ```step stage: investigate insight: "Lengths ×k, areas ×k², volumes ×k³: the more dimensions, the more the scale factor is multiplied in." tasks: - check: type: number q: "A square has area 5 cm². It is enlarged by a scale factor of 4. What is the new area? (cm²)" answer: 80 explain: "5 × 4² = 5 × 16 = 80." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What is $4 \\times 4$?", answer: 16, explain: "4 × 4 = 16." } - check: type: number q: "A box has volume 10 cm³. It is enlarged by a scale factor of 2. What is the new volume? (cm³)" answer: 80 explain: "10 × 2³ = 10 × 8 = 80." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#ray" text: "Ray enlarges a box by a scale factor of 3. Click the line where his working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: enlarge-area-times-k explain: "Line 3: area is multiplied by k², which is 9, not 3. Only lengths are multiplied by 3." ``` ### Lengths, areas, volumes ```worked \text{length} \times k :: Every side is multiplied by k. \text{area} \times k^2 :: Two directions, so k × k. \text{volume} \times k^3 :: Three directions, so k × k × k. k = 10 \Rightarrow \times 10, \times 100, \times 1000 :: The monster. ``` ### Area and volume ### Find the mistake Read Ray's working. Which line multiplies the area by k? ## Modify: change the factor ```step stage: modify insight: "Going backwards from the area or volume to the scale factor tests that k² and k³ are used the right way round." tasks: - hint: ["Area scales by k².", "k² = 100 ÷ 25."] check: { type: number, q: "A shape's area goes from $25$ cm² to $100$ cm². What is the scale factor for lengths?", answer: 2, explain: "100 ÷ 25 = 4 = k², so k = 2." } - hint: ["Volume scales by k³.", "216 = 6 × 6 × 6."] check: { type: number, q: "A model's volume is multiplied by $216$. What is the scale factor for lengths?", answer: 6, explain: "k³ = 216, so k = 6." } - hint: ["Compare the factors for strength and weight.", "Cross-section ×100, volume ×1000."] check: { type: question, q: "A shape is enlarged by a scale factor of 10. By how much is its volume multiplied?", options: ["1000", "10", "100", "30"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "10 is the factor for lengths.", "100 is the factor for area.", "k³ is 10 × 10 × 10, not 3 × 10."], explain: "10³ = 1000." } ``` ### From area to k ### From volume to k ### Volume ## Practise: scale it ```step stage: practise insight: "Using k, k² and k³ on lengths, areas and volumes." tasks: - check: type: number q: "A square has side 3 cm. Enlarge it by a scale factor of 5. What is the new area? (cm²)" answer: 225 explain: "The new side is 15, so the area is 225." - check: type: number q: "A cube has volume 4 cm³. Enlarge it by a scale factor of 3. What is the new volume? (cm³)" answer: 108 explain: "4 × 3³ = 4 × 27 = 108." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What is $3 \\times 3 \\times 3$?", answer: 27, explain: "3 × 3 × 3 = 27." } - check: type: number q: "Review: a triangle's sides are 3, 4 and 5. A similar triangle has its shortest side 9. What is its longest side?" answer: 15 explain: "The factor is 3, so 5 × 3 = 15." ``` ### Area ### Volume ### Review ## Make: the monster ```step stage: make insight: "Returning to the monster: lengths ×10, strength ×100, weight ×1000, so each bit of leg carries ten times as much." tasks: - hint: ["Weight depends on volume: ×1000.", "Strength depends on the leg's cross-section: ×100."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A model lizard is scaled up by a factor of 10. Its weight is multiplied by 1000 (volume) and a leg's strength by 100 (cross-section area). How many times more weight does each unit of leg strength carry?" steps: - ["weight $\\times 10^3 = 1000$", "volume scales by k³"] - ["strength $\\times 10^2 = 100$", "area scales by k²"] - ["$1000 \\div 100 = 10$", "weight per unit of strength"] answer: "10" answerLabel: "Times more load" tolerance: 0.001 feedback: - ["1000", "That's the weight. Compare it with the strength."] - ["100", "That's the strength. Compare it with the weight."] criteria: - "I used k² for strength." - "I used k³ for weight." - "I divided to compare them." explain: "The legs carry 10 times as much load per unit of strength, so the scaled-up lizard's legs would buckle." - check: type: question q: "So what must a real giant animal look like?" options: ["Thicker legs than a scaled-up copy, to keep up with the weight", "The same as a small animal", "Thinner legs", "Smaller overall"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The model says a scaled copy can't hold up.", "That's worse for strength.", "The question is about big animals."] explain: "Elephants have thick legs compared with a deer's. It's a model, not a real anatomy lesson." ``` ### The load ### Real giants **Also used in** - **Biology.** Small animals lose heat faster because they have more surface for their volume. - **Cooking and packaging.** Doubling a box gives eight times the volume but only four times the card. - **Next unit.** Surface area and volume of prisms and cylinders. ```teacher summary: Students use scale factor k for length, k² for area and k³ for volume (AC9M9SP02, node 2). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 6 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 12 min goals: - I can scale lengths, areas and volumes. - I can find k from an area or a volume. - I can explain why a bigger copy of an animal doesn't work. struggle: "Multiplying area by k. Ask: how many cubes now, doubling in all three directions?" before: > Students need What enlargement keeps. The one idea: each extra direction multiplies by k again. The monster is a model of area against volume, not real anatomy. Strength ∝ cross-section and weight ∝ volume are standard modelling assumptions. running: - "Predict: show of hands before the check." - "Paper: the monster question in Make is worked on paper first." stuck: - see: A student multiplies the area by the scale factor. ask: How many small squares fit when you double a 1 by 1 square? fix: Four. Draw it. stretch: Why do small animals lose heat faster than big ones? support: Linking cubes to build the 2 by 2 by 2 cube. leads: | Continues AC9M9SP02 node 2. Where it leads: Surface area and volume of prisms and cylinders. exit: q: A cube is enlarged by a scale factor of 2. By how much is its volume multiplied? a: "8." explain: | Lengths are multiplied by k, areas by k × k and volumes by k × k × k. The more dimensions, the more k appears. ```
